title: Wildfire smoke health impact quantification
bottleneck: Wildfire smoke now regularly blankets continents, but its health toll is poorly quantified: epidemiological studies lag the new exposure regime, the toxicity of smoke from burning structures versus vegetation differs in unknown ways, and indoor infiltration means even shelter-in-place guidance is unreliable. No health system has protocols for months-long smoke seasons, and the cumulative effects of repeated exposures across years are unstudied.
why_it_blocks: Smoke may already be reversing decades of air-quality gains, with mortality and morbidity costs in the tens of billions annually — yet it remains largely invisible in climate damage accounting. The evidence gap lets policymakers treat smoke as a nuisance rather than a public health emergency.
current_state: Low-cost sensor networks are mapping exposure in unprecedented detail, and researchers are building the first chronic-exposure cohorts. But health-protective standards for wildfire smoke specifically — distinct from urban PM2.5 — do not yet exist.
